title: Religion, Modesty & Touch
hook: A declined handshake, a lowered gaze or a covered head can each be an act of faith, and reading them as coldness gets both the person and the faith wrong.
why:
Religious practice shapes the body in ways that are easy to misread. A woman places her hand on her heart instead of taking an offered hand. A man keeps his eyes lowered when speaking to a woman colleague. A Sikh man's turban becomes the subject of a joke. A fasting colleague seems flat and slow in an afternoon meeting. To someone who does not know the practice, each can look like coldness, shyness, strangeness or lack of commitment.

These misreadings have consequences. They have cost people jobs, triggered court cases and, at their worst, fuelled violence. They also embarrass the well-meaning: the man left with his hand in the air, unsure whether to apologise, laugh or pretend it did not happen.

This chapter covers declined handshakes and what lies behind them, the public battles over greetings, the lowered gaze as modesty, covered heads, joined hands and bows, the conduct of holy spaces, and the effect of fasting on the body. Throughout, the rule is the same: let the other person lead, and do not assume that everyone of a faith observes it in the same way.

teach.p:
Many observant Muslims, many Orthodox Jews and members of some other religious communities avoid touching people of the opposite sex who are not close family. In Orthodox Judaism the practice is known as shomer negiah, literally observing touch. In Islam it draws on teachings about modesty and the boundaries between unrelated men and women. In both, the rule usually applies in both directions: an Orthodox Jewish man may decline a woman's hand just as an observant Muslim woman may decline a man's.

The meaning is not rejection. Those who keep these practices describe them as reserving touch for the people closest to them, giving it a meaning that casual contact would wear away. The person declining usually offers an alternative: a hand on the heart, a nod, a small bow, a warm smile and a greeting in words.

For the man whose hand is left in the air, the moment can feel like a public rebuff. The graceful response is simple. Withdraw the hand without comment, and answer the greeting that was offered: place your own hand on your heart, nod, smile, say that you are glad to meet them. Do not apologise at length, joke about it or ask for an explanation on the spot.

The figures here show the moment: a man offering his hand, a woman answering with her hand on her heart. Nothing in her greeting is cold. The warmth is all there; it simply does not travel through the hand.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if declining a handshake for religious reasons were usually a sign of personal hostility. Those who keep these practices describe them as a matter of modesty and the meaning of touch, and they offer other greetings in its place.
teach.pullQuote: The warmth is all there; it simply does not travel through the hand.

teach.p:
In some countries the handshake has become a political symbol. In 2018 Sweden's Labour Court heard the case of Farah Alhajeh, a Muslim woman who had been interviewing for a job as an interpreter. She declined to shake hands with the male interviewer and placed her hand on her heart instead, and the interview was ended. By three votes to two, the court found that she had been discriminated against and awarded her 40,000 kronor.

The court's reasoning is worth noticing. An employer could require staff to treat men and women equally, including in how they greet people, but it could not insist that the greeting be a handshake. A woman who greets everyone with a hand on her heart treats men and women alike.

The same year, Denmark passed a law requiring new citizens to shake hands with an official at their naturalisation ceremony, from January 2019. Supporters described the handshake as a sign of taking the country to heart. Critics, including many mayors who would have to carry it out, said it was aimed at Muslims and turned a courtesy into a test.

For an individual reader, the lesson is practical. Equality in greeting can be achieved by greeting everyone the same way, and there is more than one way to do it. The figure here greets with his hand on his heart, a gesture that is respectful in many cultures and gives no one a reason to decline.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if a handshake were the only way to treat people equally. Sweden's Labour Court found that greeting all people in the same way, with a hand on the heart, met the requirement of equal treatment.

teach.p:
Many religious traditions encourage modesty of the eyes. The Qur'an asks believing men and believing women to lower their gaze, and many observant Muslims avoid prolonged eye contact with unrelated people of the opposite sex. Similar norms are found among some Orthodox Jewish communities and in other traditions where the gaze is treated as a form of contact.

In practice, an observant man may look at a woman colleague's face briefly and then lower or shift his gaze while she speaks. An observant woman may do the same with a man. To someone raised to treat steady eye contact as a sign of honesty and engagement, this can look shifty, shy, uninterested or disrespectful.

The misreading matters most in high-stakes settings. A job interview, a police interview, a medical consultation or a parent-teacher meeting can turn on whether someone seems trustworthy, and a lowered gaze can count against him unfairly. Earlier chapters have already warned that eye contact is a poor guide to honesty. Here it may also be a sign of the opposite of what it seems: respect.

The figure here lowers his gaze and turns it slightly aside. Before reading it as evasion, consider who he is talking to, and what his eyes might be observing rather than avoiding.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if a lowered gaze always reflected shyness or evasion. In several religious traditions, it is an explicit practice of modesty, especially between men and women who are not related.

teach.p:
Head coverings are among the most visible signs of faith. Many Muslim women wear the hijab; many Jewish men wear a kippah; Sikh men, and some Sikh women, wear a turban, called a dastar. Each carries religious meaning, and each attracts comment, curiosity and, sometimes, hostility.

For Sikhs, the turban covers kesh, uncut hair, which is one of the five articles of faith that initiated Sikhs keep. It is not a hat or a cultural accessory. Touching a man's turban, joking about it, or asking him to remove it is deeply offensive. Days after the attacks of 11 September 2001, a Sikh man, Balbir Singh Sodhi, was shot dead at his petrol station in Arizona by a man who took him for a Muslim. Many Sikh men describe being stared at, searched more often and taunted, often by people who know nothing about their faith.

The respectful approach is to treat a head covering as part of the person. Do not touch it. Do not ask someone to remove it except where a genuine safety or identification need requires it, and then privately, with a same-sex official where possible. Questions asked out of real interest, at a suitable moment, are usually welcome; jokes are not.

The figure here, a Sikh man in a turban, greets with his palms joined and his head slightly bowed. His turban is part of who he is, as much as his name.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if head coverings were merely cultural fashion. For Sikhs, the turban covers uncut hair kept as an article of faith, and for many Muslims and Jews, head coverings are religious practice.

teach.p:
In many traditions the hands and the head do the work of greeting without touch. Hindus commonly greet with namaste or namaskar: palms pressed together in front of the chest, often with a slight bow. Many Sikhs greet with joined hands and the words Sat Sri Akal. Buddhists in many countries bow with joined hands, and the Thai wai, palms together and raised higher for those of higher status, comes from the same root.

These greetings are complete in themselves. They do not need a handshake to follow, and offering one afterwards can seem to say that the first greeting did not count. Answering in kind, with joined hands or a small bow, is understood almost everywhere and is rarely taken as presumptuous.

Bows carry their own grammar. A slight bow of the head acknowledges; a deeper bow from the waist shows greater respect. In some traditions people bow before a sacred text, an altar or an elder, and a visitor is not expected to know every rule. Following the lead of those around you, and erring on the side of slightly more respect rather than less, is usually enough.

The figure here offers a light bow, the simplest courtesy across many cultures and faiths, and one that never requires anyone to touch.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if joined hands and bows were felt as incomplete without a handshake. In the traditions that use them, they are full greetings, and answering in kind is the expected response.

teach.p:
Visiting a place of worship for a wedding, a funeral or a festival puts many men in a space whose rules they do not know. A few are widely shared. Shoes come off before entering most mosques, gurdwaras and Hindu and Buddhist temples, and a rack or room is usually provided. In a gurdwara everyone, man or woman, covers the head; scarves are usually available at the door.

Many of these spaces are used sitting on the floor. In a gurdwara, the shared meal called langar is often eaten sitting in rows on the floor, and anyone, of any faith, is welcome to it. In mosques and temples, people sit on carpets. Keeping the soles of your feet away from others, from the holy book and from the direction of prayer is a widely shared courtesy.

Other rules concern movement. In a mosque, walking directly in front of someone who is praying is avoided. In some mosques and synagogues, men and women sit separately. Photographs may not be allowed. Speaking quietly and dressing modestly, with arms and legs covered, are safe defaults almost everywhere.

The figure here sits cross-legged on the floor, feet tucked in, the way guests sit in many gurdwaras, mosques and temples. When in doubt, watch the regulars and follow them, or ask someone quietly at the door.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if places of worship had no shared conventions of the body. Removing shoes, covering the head and sitting on the floor with feet tucked away are consistent expectations across many faiths.

teach.p:
Many faiths include periods of fasting. During Ramadan, observant Muslims take no food or drink, not even water, from dawn until sunset, for about a month. Yom Kippur involves a twenty-five-hour fast. Many Christians observe Lent, and many Hindus, Jains and others fast on particular days.

Fasting shows in the body. Energy often dips in the afternoon; concentration can wander; voices can be flatter and movements slower; tempers can be shorter. Sleep is often disrupted during Ramadan by late meals and early rising. A fasting colleague who seems subdued in a four o'clock meeting is probably not bored, unhappy or disengaged. He is probably hungry, thirsty and tired.

Small adjustments help a great deal. Schedule demanding meetings earlier in the day. Do not press food or drink on someone who is fasting, and do not make a show of hiding your own lunch either; most people who fast simply want it treated as normal. Offer flexibility where you can. If you are invited to an iftar, the meal that breaks the fast at sunset, it is a generous invitation worth accepting.

The figure here sits with his hand to his face, the posture of someone tired late in the day. Before reading it as boredom, it is worth knowing what month it is.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if fasting had no noticeable effect on energy and mood. Going without food and water through a working day reliably affects alertness, especially in the afternoon.

poseGallery.doCaption: Answering with a hand on your heart
poseGallery.dontCaption: Keeping your hand out after it is declined
poseGallery.annotation: Withdraw the hand without comment and return the greeting you were offered.

poseGallery.doCaption: Accepting a lowered gaze as modesty
poseGallery.annotation: In several faiths a lowered gaze between men and women is a practice of modesty. Do not read it as evasion.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Insisting on a handshake after joined hands
poseGallery.annotation: Joined hands and a bow are a complete greeting. Answer in kind rather than adding a handshake.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Soles of the feet facing others
poseGallery.annotation: In many faiths and cultures, showing someone the soles of your feet is an insult. Keep them tucked away.

poseGallery.doCaption: A warm nod and a word of greeting
poseGallery.dontCaption: Turning away after a declined hand
poseGallery.annotation: A declined handshake is not a rebuff. Answer with a nod, a smile and a word, and carry on as you would have.

poseGallery.doCaption: A small bow to answer joined hands
poseGallery.annotation: Answering a greeting in kind is understood almost everywhere. Embarrassment makes the moment bigger than it needs to be.

caseStudy:
Gary, forty-seven, became site manager for a large housing project in a city where most of his crew and many of his clients had different faiths from his own. He considered himself easygoing, and was surprised to find himself wrong-footed three times in his first month.

The first time, he offered his hand to Mrs Begum, a client, who smiled and placed her hand on her heart. Gary froze, laughed, said sorry twice, and spent the rest of the meeting feeling awkward. The second time, during Ramadan, he noticed that Yusuf, one of his best joiners, was slow and quiet in the afternoons, and was close to raising it as a performance issue. The third time, a young apprentice made a joke about Harpreet's turban in the canteen, and Gary laughed before he had thought about it.

Harpreet took him aside the next day, not angrily, and explained what the turban meant to him and what it had been like to be stared at and taunted since he was a boy. He also told him, with a smile, about Mrs Begum's hand on her heart: it was a greeting, and Gary only had to give it back.

Gary made three changes. He now waits for clients to offer a hand, and answers whatever greeting he is given. During Ramadan he moves the heaviest work for fasting crew to the mornings and lets them finish earlier. And he told the apprentice, privately and plainly, that a man's faith is not material for jokes on his site.

At the end of the project, Yusuf invited the whole crew to an iftar at his mosque. Gary sat on the floor with his shoes off, his feet tucked under him, and his knees complaining.
observe: Notice how people in your workplace or neighbourhood greet each other, and how many do not use a handshake.
Notice your own reaction when a greeting does not go as you expected, and how you recover.
Notice head coverings around you, and whether you know what each means to the person wearing it.
Notice the calendar: when Ramadan, Yom Kippur, Lent or other fasts fall this year, and who around you might be observing them.

drills.name: The Graceful Recovery
steps: Imagine offering your hand and having it declined with a hand on the heart.
Decide in advance exactly what you will do: withdraw, place your hand on your heart, smile and greet in words.
Practise the sequence until it feels natural.
Next time you meet someone new, let them offer a hand first.
variations: Practise the recovery with a friend playing the person who declines, using a hand on the heart, a nod and joined hands in turn.
Watch how people in your workplace greet each other for a week, and notice how many already use something other than a handshake.
Practise answering joined hands with joined hands and a small bow, so that it feels natural if the moment comes.

drills.name: Faith Calendar
steps: Look up the dates of the main fasts and festivals of the faiths represented around you.
For each, note one thing that might affect work or social life, such as fasting hours or travel.
Plan one adjustment you could offer, such as earlier meetings or flexible hours.
variations: Add the fasts and festivals of your own faith or tradition to the calendar too, so that it covers everyone.
Share the calendar with whoever organises team events, with a note about which weeks to avoid for food-based celebrations.
Send a short, warm greeting to a colleague on one of their festivals, using the correct name for it.

drills.name: Visit a Holy Space
steps: Arrange to visit a place of worship of a faith other than your own, such as on an open day.
Find out in advance what to wear and how to behave.
During the visit, watch how regulars move, sit, greet and pray.
Ask one respectful question of someone who welcomes questions.
Afterwards, write down what surprised you.
variations: Before the visit, ask someone who belongs to that place of worship what a newcomer is most likely to get wrong.
After the visit, notice which of your assumptions turned out to be wrong, and which courtesies surprised you most.
If the place offers a shared meal, stay for it, and notice how the meal is served and shared.

drills.name: Ask, Don't Assume
steps: Think of a colleague or neighbour whose faith you know little about.
List what you assume about their practice of touch, food, dress and greetings.
Find a natural moment to ask one respectful question about it.
Note how much of your list was right, and how much varied from the general picture.
variations: Repeat the exercise for a faith you think you know well, and see how much of your list turns out to vary.
Ask the question in a way that makes it easy to decline, and notice whether the person chooses to answer.
Write down one practice you learned about this week that you had never heard of before.

quiz.q: A colleague says that a Muslim woman who declined to shake his hand at a meeting was being cold and rude to him. What does this chapter suggest?
options: He is right, since declining a handshake is always a personal rejection, whatever the reason
For many observant people, avoiding touch with the opposite sex is about faith, not about him
She should have shaken his hand anyway, since the customs of the workplace override her religion
He should stop greeting women altogether, so that no one is ever put in that position again
quiz.explain: Many observant Muslims and Orthodox Jews reserve touch for close family, and offer other greetings instead. Returning her hand-on-heart greeting is the graceful response.

quiz.q: What did Sweden's Labour Court decide in 2018 in the case of Farah Alhajeh?
options: Employers may require equal greetings for men and women, but may not insist on a handshake
Employers may require every member of their staff to shake hands with all visitors, men or women
Religious reasons can never justify declining a handshake in a job interview in Sweden
The case was dismissed, because a declined handshake was judged to be a private matter
quiz.explain: By three votes to two, the court found that she had been discriminated against. Greeting everyone the same way, with a hand on the heart, met the requirement to treat men and women equally.

options: A Jewish blessing said before meals, usually with the head covered and the eyes closed
An Islamic rule requiring men to keep their beards uncut from the age of adulthood onward, for life
An Orthodox Jewish practice of avoiding affectionate touch with the opposite sex outside family
A Sikh article of faith, worn as a small steel bracelet on the right wrist of the wearer
quiz.explain: Shomer negiah means observing touch. It reserves physical contact between men and women for spouses and close family, and applies to men as much as to women.

quiz.q: Why is touching or joking about a Sikh man's turban so offensive?
options: It is a fashion item that Sikh men have chosen to wear, and they are very proud of its colours
It shows a man's rank in the community, so touching it questions his social standing
It is worn only for ceremonies, and seeing it at work is a sign of a special occasion
It covers uncut hair kept as an article of faith, so it is part of his religious identity
quiz.explain: The turban covers kesh, uncut hair, one of the five articles of faith. Treating it as a hat or a joke disrespects his faith as well as the man.

quiz.q: A colleague who is fasting for Ramadan seems tired and quiet in a late-afternoon meeting. What fits this chapter best?
options: Raise his lack of engagement with him, since tiredness at work is unprofessional
Schedule demanding meetings earlier, and read his tiredness as fasting, not boredom
Insist that he takes a break to eat and drink something, for the sake of his health
Hide your own food and drink carefully, so that he is not reminded he is hungry
quiz.explain: Going without food and water all day lowers afternoon energy. Earlier meetings help, and most people who fast simply want it treated as normal.

quiz.q: You are attending a friend's wedding at a gurdwara for the first time. What fits this chapter best?
options: Keep your shoes on and stand at the back, since guests are not expected to take part
Wear a hat of your choice, since any head covering is acceptable in a holy place
Remove your shoes, cover your head, and follow others' lead in where and how to sit
Sit with your legs stretched out in front of you, since the floor is uncomfortable
quiz.explain: In a gurdwara everyone removes shoes and covers the head, and guests often sit on the floor. Watching the regulars and following them is the safest guide.

quiz.q: In 2018, Denmark passed a law about handshakes. What did it require?
options: That all employees shake hands with their managers at the start of each working day
That new citizens shake hands with an official at their naturalisation ceremony, from 2019
That nobody shake hands in public during the winter months, to reduce the spread of illness
That schools teach children to greet with a bow rather than a handshake from the age of five
quiz.explain: The law required new citizens to shake hands with an official at their naturalisation ceremony, from January 2019. The handshake had become a political symbol, which made declining it more fraught for people of faith.

quiz.q: An Orthodox Jewish client keeps his hands at his sides when a woman finance director offers hers, nods and explains that he does not shake hands for religious reasons. What fits this chapter best?
options: Read it as disrespect towards women, since he would have shaken a man's hand
Accept it warmly, knowing the practice usually applies to both sexes, and judge him on his work
Insist on the handshake, since it is the normal business greeting in this country
Ask him in front of her colleagues to explain exactly why he will not shake her hand
quiz.explain: Shomer negiah usually applies in both directions: an Orthodox Jewish man avoids touching women outside close family, and an observant Jewish woman avoids touching men. It reserves touch for the closest relationships and says nothing about her status.

quiz.q: Someone says a Muslim colleague who shakes hands and does not wear a headscarf cannot really be observant. What does this chapter suggest?
options: That observance varies within every faith, and how someone practises is their own business
That every observant Muslim follows exactly the same rules on dress and touch in every setting
That a colleague's observance should be checked before they are invited to faith-based events
That shaking hands is always forbidden in Islam, so the colleague must not be Muslim at all
quiz.explain: People of the same faith observe it in very different ways, shaped by family, conscience and community. Measuring someone against your idea of their faith either finds them lacking or marks them out.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific moment when religious practice shaped a nonverbal exchange you were part of: a declined handshake, a lowered gaze, a head covering, a fast, a visit to a place of worship. Describe what each person did with their body, how you read it at the time, and how you would read it now. If you are religious yourself, describe one practice of yours that others have misread, and what you wish they had understood.
reflection.guidance: Many people feel awkward about religion, afraid of saying the wrong thing. Write honestly about your reactions, including discomfort, and focus on specific behaviour rather than on beliefs. Remember that observance varies widely within every faith, so avoid generalising from one person to everyone who shares their religion.

failureMode: The first failure is to read a declined handshake as a personal rebuff, and to recover badly: freezing, joking, over-apologising or asking for an explanation. The second is to insist on the handshake as the only proper greeting. The third is to read a lowered gaze as evasion or shyness when it is modesty. The fourth is to treat a turban, a hijab or a kippah as fair game for touch, jokes or casual demands. The fifth is to break the rules of a holy space through ignorance: shoes on, head bare, feet pointed. The sixth is to read a fasting colleague's tiredness as disengagement. And the seventh is to assume that every member of a faith observes it in the same way.

moreCases.title: The accountant who did not shake her hand
moreCases.scene:
Avi, thirty-five, is an accountant and an Orthodox Jew. He keeps shomer negiah: he does not touch women other than his wife and close family, and does not shake their hands. He has a new client, Kate, forty-two, finance director of a manufacturing company, and they meet for the first time in her office.

Kate stands, smiles and holds out her hand. Avi smiles back, keeps his hands at his sides, inclines his head slightly and says warmly, "It's very good to meet you, Kate. I hope you don't mind, I don't shake hands, for religious reasons." Kate lowers her hand. Her smile stays, but something in her face closes.

For the first ten minutes of the meeting, she is brisk and slightly cool. She has spent twenty years in rooms where men talked over her and addressed their questions to her junior male colleagues, and her first reading is that this is another man who does not respect women.

Afterwards, she mentions it to her deputy, Sanjay, who has worked with Orthodox Jewish clients before. He tells her that the practice applies in both directions: Avi would not shake hands with any woman, and an observant Jewish woman would not shake his. He adds that Avi's firm is known for having more women partners than most.

Avi has had this moment many times, and he has learned to say his sentence early and warmly, before the other person's hand is fully out. Sometimes it works. Sometimes, as now, the other person's face closes anyway.

Kate's office has a framed photograph on the wall of the company's first all-woman board, of which she is very proud. Avi noticed it as he came in, and admired it, which she did not notice.

Later in the meeting, when Kate's junior colleague, Tom, joins them, Avi greets him with a handshake. Kate notices, and her first reading hardens for a moment, until she reminds herself to wait and see.
moreCases.misread:
Kate read Avi's declined handshake as disrespect towards women, drawing on long experience of men who had shown exactly that. She did not know that the practice was symmetrical, and had nothing to do with her status or her work.

She also read his small bow and his warmth as politeness covering the slight, when they were the whole of his greeting.

Avi, for his part, read the coolness in the first ten minutes accurately, as a woman who had taken the greeting badly, and worked hard to show by everything else he did that he respected her, which he did.

Tom, the junior colleague, read none of it, because he had never seen Kate's face close before and did not know what it meant.
moreCases.betterRead:
This chapter describes how many Orthodox Jews and many observant Muslims avoid touching people of the opposite sex outside close family, and that the rule usually applies in both directions. The meaning, for those who keep it, is reserving touch for the closest relationships, not rejection. Avi did what the chapter suggests: he declined warmly, early, with a smile, a small bow and a sentence of explanation. Kate's reading was understandable, given her history, and wrong. Her better reading, once Sanjay had explained, was to judge Avi on how he treated her in the work, which turned out to be with respect: he addressed his questions to her, deferred to her decisions and copied her on everything. At their next meeting, she greeted him with a nod and "Good to see you, Avi," and he said later that it was the first time a new client had made the greeting easy for him.

Sanjay also suggested that the firm's client guidance mention greetings, so that nobody else had to learn it in the moment.

moreCases.title: The candidate who lowered his eyes
moreCases.scene:
Bilal, twenty-six, is an observant Muslim and a recent engineering graduate, interviewing for a graduate scheme at a transport company. The panel is three people: two men and a woman, Claire, a senior engineer. Bilal makes good eye contact with the two men. When Claire asks him a question, he looks at her briefly, then lowers or shifts his gaze to the table while he answers, glancing up now and then.

His answers to Claire's questions are strong: a clear account of a group project, a sensible approach to a safety problem. But Claire comes away uneasy. She writes "evasive with me" and "possible issue working with women" in her notes, and scores his teamwork answer lower than the men do.

In the panel discussion, one of the men, Raheem, who is also Muslim, reads Claire's notes and asks whether she noticed that Bilal lowered his gaze only with her. She says yes; that was the problem. Raheem explains that many observant Muslims, men and women, lower their gaze with unrelated people of the opposite sex as a matter of modesty, and that it is usually a sign of respect, not avoidance.

Claire looks at her notes again. She realises that she has scored a man down for being polite to her in a way she did not recognise.

Bilal had in fact been worried about exactly this before the interview, and had discussed it with his older sister, who told him to be himself and trust the panel to be fair.

Raheem had noticed it during the interview, and had made a note to raise it if Claire's scores were lower, because he had seen the same thing happen to his younger brother at a previous company.

Claire also realises, going back over her notes, that she had written nothing about Bilal's answers to her questions, only about his eyes. The answers, when she remembers them, were the best she heard that day.
moreCases.misread:
Claire read Bilal's lowered gaze, shown only with her, as evasion and a possible problem with women colleagues. It was the opposite: a form of modesty and respect that she had not met before.

The two men on the panel had not noticed the difference in gaze at all, because Bilal had looked them in the eye, and so had no reason to wonder.

And Bilal, watching Claire's face during the interview, read her coolness as a sign that she did not like him, and became more careful, which made his gaze drop further.
moreCases.betterRead:
The Qur'an asks believing men and believing women to lower their gaze, and many observant Muslims avoid prolonged eye contact with unrelated people of the opposite sex, as this chapter describes. In a high-stakes setting such as an interview, that norm is easily misread as shiftiness, and the misreading can decide the outcome. Bilal's behaviour told Claire about his faith, not about his honesty or his attitude to women. The better reading, which the panel reached, was the structured one: score what he said against the criteria agreed in advance. Claire rescored his teamwork answer on its content, which was strong. She also suggested that the company's interviewer guidance should mention that gaze varies with faith and culture, as Part IV's chapter on interviews describes. Bilal was offered a place. In his first year, his team lead was a woman, and the two worked very well together.

Claire also told Bilal, months later, about her first reading of the interview, and he laughed and said that his mother would have been horrified.

Raheem said afterwards that he was glad the panel had a way to talk about it that did not depend on him being in the room.

moreCases.title: The funeral at the gurdwara
moreCases.scene:
Steve, fifty, is a warehouse manager, and his deputy of fifteen years, Harjit, has lost his father. Steve has known Harjit's father, who used to bring homemade samosas to the warehouse at Christmas, and he wants to go to the funeral. It is at a gurdwara, and Steve has never been inside one.

He arrives in a dark suit. At the entrance, he sees people taking off their shoes and placing them on racks, and he does the same, a little awkwardly. Inside, he notices that everyone, men and women, has their head covered, and that he is the only person with a bare head. A young man at the door quietly offers him an orange scarf from a basket and shows him how to tie it. Steve thanks him.

In the prayer hall, people sit on the carpeted floor, men on one side and women on the other. Steve sits at the back with his legs stretched out in front of him, because his knees will not fold, and the soles of his feet point towards the front of the hall, where the holy book rests. An older man beside him leans over and, very gently, shows him how to sit with his legs to one side.

Afterwards, everyone is invited to langar, the shared meal, sitting in rows on the floor. Steve hesitates, unsure whether it is meant for guests.

Steve had thought about looking up what to do before he came, and decided that it would be fine. He wishes, now, that he had spent ten minutes finding out.

He notices, too, that nobody seems to mind his mistakes. Several people nod to him, and one woman, Harjit's aunt, comes over to thank him for coming, and tells him that her brother always spoke well of him.

He notices that the hall is full of people of every age, and that the children run between the rows during the meal while the adults eat and talk. It is less formal than he had expected, and warmer.
moreCases.misread:
Steve read the unfamiliar rules of the space as things he might be judged for getting wrong, and nearly left before the meal because he was not sure he belonged there. The people around him read his mistakes as the honest errors of a guest who had come to pay respect.

And he read the young man's offer of a scarf as a correction, when it was a welcome. Communities that ask visitors to cover their heads usually keep a basket of scarves for exactly this reason.

The older man who showed him how to sit read Steve's outstretched legs as a sore-kneed stranger who did not know, which was exactly right, and helped without a word of reproach.

Harjit's family, watching him struggle to sit, read his discomfort as effort, and the effort as respect, which was the reading that mattered.
moreCases.betterRead:
This chapter describes the courtesies of holy spaces: shoes off, heads covered in a gurdwara, the soles of the feet kept away from others and from the holy book, and langar offered to anyone of any faith. Steve broke two of the rules without knowing, and the people around him corrected him with the kindness that most communities show a sincere visitor. The better approach, for anyone in his position, is to find out in advance where possible, as the Visit a Holy Space drill suggests, and to watch and follow when not. Steve stayed for langar. Harjit found him in the row, sitting awkwardly with his knees to one side and a plate of dal, and sat down beside him. He told Steve later that seeing him there, in a borrowed scarf, had been one of the few comforts of the day. Steve looked up what to do before his next visit, to a colleague's wedding.

He also sent Harjit a card a week later, with a note about the samosas, which Harjit put on his father's photograph.

moreCases.title: The patient who asked for a woman
moreCases.scene:
Dominic, thirty-three, is a nurse in a hospital emergency department. On a busy night, he is assigned to a patient, Fatima, forty, who has come in with abdominal pain and needs an examination and an electrocardiogram, which involves placing electrodes on her chest. Fatima wears a hijab and a long dress. When Dominic introduces himself and explains what he needs to do, she looks uncomfortable and asks quietly whether a female nurse could do the examination.

Dominic is tired and stretched, and his first reaction is irritation, and then a small sting of hurt. He has been a nurse for ten years. He wonders whether she thinks he is going to behave inappropriately, or whether she simply does not trust male nurses. He says, a little shortly, that there is only one female nurse on the shift and that she is busy.

Fatima says she understands, and then goes quiet. She keeps her arms folded across her body. When Dominic leaves the cubicle to fetch a machine, she calls her sister on the phone, speaking quickly and anxiously.

The nurse in charge, Grace, sees Dominic's face as he comes out and asks what is wrong. He tells her. Grace says she will swap him for the next patient, and that it is not about him.

Fatima had been in two minds about asking at all, because the last time she asked for a female doctor, the receptionist had sighed loudly. She had nearly said nothing.

Dominic also realises, later, that he had introduced himself while standing over her trolley with the electrodes already in his hand, which may have made the request harder for her to make.

Grace mentions, as she swaps him, that she has had patients refuse her too, for being a woman, a nurse rather than a doctor, or too young, and that she has learned not to take any of it home.
moreCases.misread:
Dominic read Fatima's request for a female nurse as a judgment on him, perhaps as distrust of men, and responded with a shortness that made her more anxious. Fatima read his reaction as a sign that her request was a burden she should not have made.

Dominic also read his own hurt as information about her view of him, when it was a tired man taking a reasonable request personally.

Her sister, on the phone, read Fatima's anxiety as fear of the examination, when it was the fear of having made a fuss and being treated worse for it.
moreCases.betterRead:
Many observant Muslim women, and women of other faiths and none, prefer a clinician of the same sex for intimate care, as part of the modesty this chapter describes, and many hospitals have policies to accommodate such requests where possible. The request was about her faith and her body, not about Dominic. Grace's better response was to accommodate it without fuss, as she would for any patient who asked. The female nurse examined Fatima twenty minutes later. When that was not possible on other nights, Dominic learned to offer what he could: a female chaperone, a clear explanation of each step before he did it, covering everything except the area he needed, and asking permission before touching. He found that most patients who asked for a woman were grateful for those small things, and that none of it had ever been about him.

He also asked Grace whether the department could keep a note of which female staff were on each shift, so that requests could be met quickly and without anyone having to feel like a burden.

workedReading.title: Planning a team lunch during Ramadan
workedReading.scene:
Karen, forty-five, is the office manager for a design firm of forty people, and she has been asked to organise a lunch to celebrate a big contract win. The managing director wants it next week. Karen checks the calendar and sees that next week falls in Ramadan, and she knows that at least five colleagues are Muslim. She also knows that two colleagues are Orthodox Jewish, that one is vegetarian for religious reasons, and that the office includes people of several other faiths and none. She does not want to throw a party that a fifth of the office cannot enjoy, and she does not want to make a fuss that singles anyone out. She has read the Faith Calendar drill in this chapter, and she decides to start by asking rather than guessing.

She also remembers that last year's Christmas party had included a meal and a free bar, and that several colleagues had stayed for half an hour and left. Nobody had asked why.

She also remembers a colleague from a previous job who left after two years and said, on her last day, that she had never once been able to eat at a work celebration. Karen had not known, and had not asked.

She is also aware that some colleagues of no faith have their own needs, such as being teetotal, and that the planning should cover them too.

steps.label: Check the calendar
steps.text:
She looks up the dates of Ramadan and Eid for this year, and of any other fasts and festivals in the coming months. She sees that Eid al-Fitr falls about ten days after the proposed lunch. She notes that a lunch during Ramadan would mean that fasting colleagues would be sitting at a table full of food they cannot eat, during the hours when they are most tired and hungry.

She also notes the dates of Diwali, Passover, Vaisakhi and Christmas, so that the calendar is not about one faith but about the whole office.

She also checks whether any colleagues observe the Sabbath, which might rule out a Friday evening event for some of them.

steps.label: Ask, without singling anyone out
steps.text:
She sends a short message to the whole office: "We're planning a celebration for the contract win. Are there any dates, times or food needs I should know about? Reply to me directly." Several people reply. Two Muslim colleagues suggest that an evening meal after sunset would be lovely, or a celebration after Eid. The Orthodox Jewish colleagues ask whether the food could be kosher or vegetarian.

She also makes sure the message goes to everyone, so that nobody feels that they have been singled out because of their faith.

She also makes it clear in the message that people do not need to say why they have a particular need, only what it is.

She also receives one reply from a colleague who simply says, "Thanks for asking, nobody ever has," which she keeps.

steps.label: Plan food and timing
steps.text:
Karen proposes two options to the managing director: an evening celebration a fortnight later, after Eid, with a mixture of halal, kosher and vegetarian food clearly labelled, or a lunch now for those who want it and a separate iftar meal later. He chooses the celebration after Eid, and suggests calling it a joint celebration of the contract and Eid, which Karen checks with her Muslim colleagues first. They are pleased.

She also checks with the caterer that the halal and kosher food will be prepared and served separately, which matters to the people who will eat it.

She also checks the venue's kitchen practices with a colleague who keeps kosher, rather than assuming that a label on the menu is enough.

steps.label: Think about greetings and space
steps.text:
For the evening, she arranges a room large enough for people to stand or sit as they like, and asks the venue whether there is a quiet room that could be used for prayer, since the event will run past sunset prayer time. She mentions to the managing director that not everyone shakes hands across genders, and that a nod and a warm word work for everyone.

She also makes sure there are plenty of soft drinks and alcohol-free options, displayed as prominently as the wine, so that nobody has to ask.

She also makes sure the prayer room is clean, quiet and has a few chairs as well as floor space, and that the direction for prayer is marked, after asking a Muslim colleague what would be helpful.

steps.label: Keep it ordinary
steps.text:
She labels the food clearly without putting signs on tables that announce which colleagues need which food. She avoids making speeches about diversity. She simply makes sure that everyone can eat, drink, sit and take part without having to ask or explain, which is what this chapter means by making accommodation ordinary.

She also avoids asking any colleague to give a talk about their faith at the event, which would have turned a celebration into a lesson.

She also avoids any decoration that would make the event look like a theme party, which several colleagues had found uncomfortable at a previous firm.

She also asks the managing director to keep his speech short and about the contract, so that the celebration is about the work and the people, not about anyone's faith.

steps.label: On the night, follow the lead
steps.text:
At the celebration, Karen watches how people greet each other and follows their lead. When one colleague greets her with a hand on his heart, she returns it. When an older guest, a client, bows slightly with joined hands, she returns the gesture. She notices that the room is louder and happier than any work event she can remember.

She also notices that one of the Orthodox colleagues greets women with a nod and men with a handshake, and follows his lead without comment.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
Several colleagues tell Karen that it is the first work celebration they have been able to enjoy fully, and one brings her a box of sweets the following week as an Eid gift. The managing director asks Karen to put the faith calendar into the firm's planning for every year. She does, and adds a note about which weeks to avoid for big lunches, which saves the next organiser from having to work it out alone.

She also hears, a month later, that a neighbouring firm has adopted the same approach after one of her colleagues mentioned it to a friend there.

She also notices that two colleagues who rarely come to work socials came to this one, and stayed until the end.

moreFailures.title: Asking someone to explain their faith on the spot
moreFailures.body:
When someone declines a handshake, lowers their gaze, wears a head covering or does not eat at lunch, a common response is to ask, right then and in front of others, why. "Why don't you shake hands?" "Isn't it hot in that?" "Can't you just have a little?" Curiosity is natural, but the question turns a private practice into a public explanation, and puts the person in the position of defending their faith, often in a few seconds, often to someone who has just been surprised by it. It can also feel like a challenge, especially when the tone suggests that the practice needs justifying. If you are curious, wait for a natural, private moment and ask in a way that makes it easy to decline: "I'd love to know more about that sometime, if you're happy to tell me." Then listen, and do not argue with the answer.

And if you already asked, and the person looked uncomfortable, a simple "Sorry, that was nosy of me" is enough.

A good rule is that a question about someone's faith should cost them nothing to refuse.

moreFailures.title: Commenting on someone's observance
moreFailures.body:
People of the same faith observe it in very different ways, as this chapter's last failure warns, and it is tempting to comment when someone does not fit your expectations: "You're not very religious, then," to a Muslim colleague who shakes hands; "I didn't know you were Jewish, you don't look it," to someone who mentions a festival; "Do you have to wear that?" to a woman in a hijab. Each comment measures the person against your idea of what their faith requires, and either finds them lacking or marks them out. How someone practises their faith is their own business, shaped by family, conscience and many other things you cannot see. If they tell you about it, listen. Otherwise, treat their choices, whatever they are, as you would any colleague's: without remark.

The same applies to people who leave a faith or change their practice. Their reasons are theirs.

It also helps to remember that faith can change over a lifetime, and that the person in front of you may be practising differently now than they did five years ago.

moreFailures.title: Making a show of accommodation
moreFailures.body:
Wanting to be considerate, some people make their accommodation of others' faith very visible: hiding their sandwiches ostentatiously in front of a fasting colleague, announcing to the room that the Muslim guests will need somewhere to pray, putting a sign on a table saying "Halal food for our Muslim colleagues", or apologising elaborately every time they eat near someone who is fasting. It is meant kindly. It can embarrass the person it is meant to help, single them out in front of others and turn their practice into an event. Most people who fast, cover or pray simply want to get on with their day. The better approach is the one Karen took: make the accommodation ordinary and quiet, so that people can use it without having to ask, explain or be noticed, and then behave normally.

A good test is whether the person would have to be noticed in order to use the accommodation. If so, find a quieter way.

If you are unsure whether an accommodation draws attention, ask one person who would use it what they would prefer.

moreFailures.title: Reading modest dress as distance
moreFailures.body:
Modest dress, a long skirt, long sleeves, a headscarf, a loose shirt buttoned to the neck, is part of practice in many faiths, among men as well as women. To someone unfamiliar with it, it can be read as reserve, coldness, disapproval of others or a sign that the person does not want to be approached. None of these follows. A woman in a hijab may be the funniest person in the office; a man who keeps his arms covered may be the warmest. Modest dress tells you about a person's faith and choices, not about their personality or their view of you. Read the person as you would anyone: by what they say, how they treat others, and how they respond when you are friendly. As with every signal in this book, the clothing is a piece of information, not a verdict.

It also helps to remember that many people dress modestly for reasons other than faith, such as comfort, family or style.

questions.q: What should I do if someone declines my handshake for religious reasons?
questions.a:
Withdraw your hand smoothly, without comment, and answer with a greeting of your own: a nod, a smile, a hand on your heart if that feels natural, and a warm word, such as "It's lovely to meet you." Do not freeze, joke, apologise more than once or ask why, all of which turn a small moment into a large one. The Graceful Recovery drill in this chapter rehearses this sequence so that it comes naturally. Remember that the person declining is not rejecting you; they are following a practice that, for many, reserves touch for the people closest to them, and that usually applies in both directions, as Kate learned. Then carry on with the meeting exactly as you would have, and judge the person on everything else they do.

And if you are the one declining, saying your sentence early and warmly, as Avi did, makes it easier for the other person to follow.

And if you are a woman whose hand is declined by a man, it may help to know that he would decline any woman's, and that it is not a judgment of you.

questions.q: Should I offer my hand at all?
questions.a:
In many settings, the simplest approach is to let the other person lead, as Gary learned to do on his site. Walk up with your hands relaxed, ready to shake if a hand is offered, and ready to nod, bow slightly or return a hand on the heart if not. If you do offer first and it is declined, recover gracefully. In some workplaces with many people who do not shake hands across genders, people have simply adopted a nod and a warm word as the normal greeting for everyone, which avoids the question altogether. The chapter on handshakes in Part IV describes the post-pandemic world in which offering slowly and reading the other person's hand has become ordinary practice for everyone, which helps here too.

In mixed groups, following the most senior person's greeting is often a safe guide.

And if you find yourself frozen with your hand out, a smile and a light "Lovely to meet you" covers almost everything.

questions.q: How can I find out what someone's faith involves without being intrusive?
questions.a:
Read first, using good introductions to the major faiths, such as those listed at the end of this chapter, so that you know the basics. Notice the calendar, as the Faith Calendar drill suggests. Then, if you know someone well enough, ask at a natural, private moment, in a way that makes it easy for them to decline: "I'd love to understand more about Ramadan, if you're happy to tell me." Many people are glad to explain, and some are tired of doing so; let them decide. Remember that practice varies a great deal within every faith, so what one person tells you may not apply to the next. And ask practical questions when they matter, such as "Is there anything you'd like me to know about food or timing for the team lunch?"

It also helps to accept that you will never know everything, and that a sincere wish to learn is usually received far better than expertise.

If someone does tell you about their practice, thank them, and remember what they said, so that they do not have to explain twice.

questions.q: Is it all right to ask about or compliment someone's head covering?
questions.a:
A genuine compliment, such as "That's a beautiful scarf," is usually welcome, as it would be about anyone's clothing. Questions are best kept for a private moment and a person you know, and best asked with curiosity rather than challenge: "Can I ask what the turban means to you?" rather than "Isn't it uncomfortable?" Never touch someone's head covering without being invited, and never ask someone to remove it, which for many is deeply offensive. This chapter describes the turban as covering kesh, uncut hair, one of the five articles of faith for initiated Sikhs, and describes the hostility Sikh men often face. Jokes about head coverings, however light, are never appropriate, and if you hear them, the quiet interruption described in the chapter on the queer nonverbal dialect works here too.

It also helps to know that many people wear head coverings for reasons of faith that are personal and varied, even within one tradition.

questions.q: How can I support a colleague who is fasting?
questions.a:
Mostly by adjusting quietly rather than making a fuss. Schedule demanding meetings and heavy work earlier in the day where you can, since energy often dips in the afternoon. Offer flexibility, such as starting and finishing earlier, if your workplace allows it. Do not press food or drink on them, and do not make a show of hiding your own; most people who fast simply want to get on with their day. Avoid planning team lunches or celebrations with food during the fast, or offer an alternative, as Karen did. Do not read tiredness, quietness or a short temper in the late afternoon as disengagement, as Gary nearly did with Yusuf. And if your colleague invites you to an iftar, the meal that breaks the fast, go if you can; it is usually a warm and generous occasion.

It also helps to wish them a good Eid when the fast ends, using the name of the festival, which many people appreciate.

It also helps to remember that not every Muslim colleague fasts, for reasons of health, pregnancy or choice, and that nobody needs to explain.

questions.q: What if a religious practice seems to conflict with workplace rules?
questions.a:
Look for the purpose of the rule, and ask whether the practice actually conflicts with it. Sweden's Labour Court, in the 2018 case of Farah Alhajeh, found that an employer could require staff to treat men and women equally in how they greet people, but could not insist that the greeting be a handshake; a woman who greeted everyone with a hand on her heart treated men and women alike. The same reasoning often helps elsewhere: a rule about professional appearance can usually accommodate a head covering, and a rule about meetings can usually accommodate prayer times or a fast. Talk to the person about what they need and what the role requires. Laws on religious discrimination vary between countries, so in a genuine conflict, take advice from human resources or a legal adviser.

Most conflicts dissolve when both sides focus on what the rule is for, rather than on the form it usually takes.

And remember that most people of faith are well used to fitting their practice around work, and will meet a reasonable employer more than halfway.
